title: Indexes and constraints
summary: Unique indexes, composite indexes, check constraints and default values: rules the database keeps for you.

steps.title: Indexes
body: Without an index, `WHERE "Email" = 'a@b.c'` reads every row. An **index** is a sorted copy of one or more columns that lets the database jump straight to the matches, like the index at the back of a book.
A **unique** index is also a rule: no two rows may share an email. This is how you keep a natural value unique while using a generated key.
Indexes are not free: every insert and update must maintain them too. Add them for columns you **filter, join or sort on**, not for every column. The primary key is always indexed already.

code: catch (DbUpdateException e) when (e.InnerException is SqliteException { SqliteErrorCode: 19 })
protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder options) => options.UseSqlite("Data Source=club.db");
steps.explain: The second insert breaks the unique index. SQLite reports error 19 (a constraint failed), which EF Core wraps in a `DbUpdateException`. The failed row is never stored. `ChangeTracker.Clear()` drops the still-pending `Added` entity so the context is clean again.

steps.title: Composite indexes and constraints
body: An index can cover several columns. Order matters: an index on `(LastName, FirstName)` helps `WHERE LastName = ...` and `WHERE LastName = ... AND FirstName = ...`, but not `WHERE FirstName = ...` alone, just as a phone book sorted by surname does not help you find every "Ana".
Two more rules the database can keep:
A **check constraint** is a SQL condition every row must satisfy. A **default value** is used when the insert does not supply one.

steps.prompt: You have an index on `(City, Street)`. Which query can use it best?
steps.explain: A composite index is sorted by its first column, then the next. It helps queries that start from the left: `City`, or `City` and `Street`. `Street` alone would have to scan the whole index.

steps.explain: `SaveChanges` runs in a transaction. The second insert breaks the check constraint, so the whole save is rolled back: not even Dune was stored.

steps.prompt: The registration endpoint already checks `AnyAsync(a => a.Username == name)` before inserting. Why still add a unique index?
options: Two requests can both pass the check at the same moment; only the database can guarantee uniqueness
The index makes the check unnecessary to write
EF Core ignores the check without an index
SQLite requires an index on every string column
steps.explain: Check-then-insert is a race. The check gives a friendly message in the common case; the unique index is what makes a duplicate impossible, and turns the race into a `DbUpdateException` you can map to 409.

steps.title: Rules for usernames
prompt: Write an `Account` entity and an `AppDb` context (`Data Source=app.db`, `DbSet<Account> Accounts`):

Then write `bool TryRegister(AppDb db, string username, int age)` (at the top of your code) that adds an account and saves it. It returns `false`, leaving the context clean, when the database refuses the row.
starter: bool TryRegister(AppDb db, string username, int age)
solution: bool TryRegister(AppDb db, string username, int age)
db.Accounts.Add(new Account { Username = username, Age = age });
public string Plan { get; set; } = null!;
protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder options) => options.UseSqlite("Data Source=app.db");
template: Dojo.Check("Username has a unique index", dojoSql.Contains("CREATE UNIQUE INDEX") && dojoSql.Contains("(\"Username\")"), dojoSql);
Dojo.Check("the age check constraint exists", dojoSql.Contains("CK_Accounts_Age"), dojoSql);
Dojo.Check("Plan defaults to free", dojoSql.Contains("DEFAULT 'free'"), dojoSql);
Dojo.Eq("a second ana is refused", false, TryRegister(dojoDb, "ana", 40));
Dojo.Eq("ben (13) registers after the failures", true, TryRegister(dojoDb, "ben", 13));
Dojo.Eq("two accounts are stored", new List<string> { "ana", "ben" }, dojoDb.Accounts.OrderBy(a => a.Id).Select(a => a.Username).ToList());
Dojo.Eq("the database filled in the plan", "free", dojoDb.Accounts.First().Plan);
hints: Catch `DbUpdateException`, then `db.ChangeTracker.Clear()` so the refused account is not retried on the next save.
If `Plan` has a C# default like `""`, EF Core sends that instead of letting the database default apply: use `= null!`.
